claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure.
The starting alloy exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle failure.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations and premature microcracking in the starting alloy.
Minor-element doping should be introduced by co-deposition or infiltration at 1000–1100°C in an inert atmosphere.
Elevated-temperature doping for sufficient time will produce a uniform distribution of minor alloying additions.
Minor-element doping modifies and strengthens the alloy's internal boundaries.
Dopant-modified boundary chemistry reduces dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Dopant-modified boundaries enable smoother dislocation transfer across interfaces.
Increasing boundary cohesion reduces microcrack initiation at interphase boundaries.
Reduced microcrack initiation improves load sharing and lowers the probability of brittle tensile failure.
Minor-element doping will increase tensile elongation by more than 10% relative to the untreated alloy.
Minor-element doping will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The beneficial doping effects will persist during room-temperature tensile testing at moderate strain rates.
The outcome depends on dopant identity, dopant concentration, diffusion kinetics, and accompanying microstructural evolution.
Failure to improve boundary cohesion or to achieve equal-or-better strength and ductility than an undoped control would refute the hypothesis.
